title: Distance Formula & Collinearity Criteria: Pythogorean Derivation & Geometric Classifications
description: Rigorously derive the Distance Formula d = √[(x₂ - x₁)² + (y₂ - y₁)²] using the Pythagorean theorem on Cartesian projections. Master testing for collinearity via segment addition (AB + BC = AC) and classifying geometric figures (equilateral/isosceles triangles, squares, rectangles, rhombuses).
key_concepts: Cartesian Projection: Horizontal distance Δx = |x₂ - x₁|, Vertical distance Δy = |y₂ - y₁|
Pythagorean Derivation: In right triangle PRQ, PQ² = PR² + RQ² ⇒ d = √[(x₂ - x₁)² + (y₂ - y₁)²]
Distance from Origin: d(O, P) = √(x² + y²)
Collinearity Criterion: Points A, B, C are collinear if and only if the sum of lengths of any two segments equals the third (e.g. AB + BC = AC)
Geometric Quadrilateral Criteria: Parallelogram (opposite sides equal), Rhombus (all 4 sides equal), Rectangle (opposite sides equal + diagonals equal), Square (all 4 sides equal + diagonals equal)
subtopics: Full algebraic derivation of the distance formula
Distance between symbolic points (a, b) and (-a, -b)
Equidistant point condition on axes: On x-axis (x, 0), on y-axis (0, y)

worked_examples.problem: Example 1 (NCERT): Do the points (3, 2), (-2, -3) and (2, 3) form a triangle? If so, name the type of triangle formed.
worked_examples.solution:
Let the given points be P(3, 2), Q(-2, -3), and R(2, 3).
Formula: Distance d = √[ (x₂ - x₁)² + (y₂ - y₁)² ]

Step 1: Calculate length PQ:
PQ = √[ (-2 - 3)² + (-3 - 2)² ] = √[ (-5)² + (-5)² ] = √[ 25 + 25 ] = √50 ≈ 7.07 units.

Step 2: Calculate length QR:
QR = √[ (2 - (-2))² + (3 - (-3))² ] = √[ 4² + 6² ] = √[ 16 + 36 ] = √52 ≈ 7.21 units.

Step 3: Calculate length PR:
PR = √[ (2 - 3)² + (3 - 2)² ] = √[ (-1)² + 1² ] = √[ 1 + 1 ] = √2 ≈ 1.41 units.

Step 4: Check Triangle Inequality Theorem:
The sum of any two lengths must be strictly greater than the third length:
PQ + PR = 7.07 + 1.41 = 8.48 > 7.21 (QR)
PQ + QR = 7.07 + 7.21 = 14.28 > 1.41 (PR)
QR + PR = 7.21 + 1.41 = 8.62 > 7.07 (PQ)
Since the sum of any two sides is greater than the third, the points P, Q, R form a triangle.

Step 5: Check for Right-Angled Triangle via Converse of Pythagoras Theorem:
PQ² + PR² = (√50)² + (√2)² = 50 + 2 = 52.
QR² = (√52)² = 52.
Since PQ² + PR² = QR², by the converse of Pythagoras Theorem, ΔPQR is a right-angled triangle with hypotenuse QR (right angle at P).
[ROUGH_WORK]
50 + 2 = 52
Converse of Pythagoras holds exactly!
Boxed Answer: [ Yes, the points form a Right-Angled Triangle with ∠P = 90° ].
concept_questions: What would it mean if PQ + PR was exactly equal to QR?
Why does the distance formula produce identical results if you swap the order of the points (x₁ - x₂)²?

worked_examples.problem: Example 4 (NCERT): Find a relation between x and y such that the point (x, y) is equidistant from the points (7, 1) and (3, 5).
worked_examples.solution:
Let P(x, y) be the point equidistant from A(7, 1) and B(3, 5).
Given condition: PA = PB
Squaring both sides (to eliminate the square root radical): PA² = PB²

Formula: PA² = (x - 7)² + (y - 1)²
PB² = (x - 3)² + (y - 5)²

Step 1: Equate PA² and PB²:
(x - 7)² + (y - 1)² = (x - 3)² + (y - 5)²

Step 2: Expand all binomials using (a - b)² = a² - 2ab + b²:
(x² - 14x + 49) + (y² - 2y + 1) = (x² - 6x + 9) + (y² - 10y + 25)
x² + y² - 14x - 2y + 50 = x² + y² - 6x - 10y + 34

Step 3: Cancel x² and y² from both sides:
-14x - 2y + 50 = -6x - 10y + 34
Move all terms to LHS:
-14x + 6x - 2y + 10y + 50 - 34 = 0
-8x + 8y + 16 = 0

Step 4: Divide entire equation by -8:
x - y - 2 = 0 (or x - y = 2).
[ROUGH_WORK]
Geometric Meaning: The set of all points equidistant from A and B is the perpendicular bisector of segment AB!
Midpoint of AB: ((7+3)/2, (1+5)/2) = (5, 3).
Check (5, 3): 5 - 3 = 2 (True!)
Boxed Answer: [ The relation between x and y is x - y = 2 (which represents the perpendicular bisector of segment AB) ].
concept_questions: Why did x² and y² cancel out completely?
What is the geometric locus represented by x - y = 2?

title: Section Formula & Internal Division: Masterclass in m₁ : m₂ Coordinates, Trisection & Midpoints
description: Rigorously derive the Section Formula using similar right triangles. Master finding dividing coordinates P(x, y), calculating the unknown ratio k : 1, trisection coordinates, and the midpoint formula.
key_concepts: Section Formula: P(x, y) = [ (m₁x₂ + m₂x₁) / (m₁ + m₂), (m₁y₂ + m₂y₁) / (m₁ + m₂) ]
Derivation via Similar Triangles: Horizontal and vertical projections are in ratio m₁ : m₂
Special Case: Midpoint Formula M = [ (x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2 ] (when m₁ = m₂ = 1)
Unknown Ratio Technique: Let ratio be k : 1 ⇒ P = [ (kx₂ + x₁)/(k + 1), (ky₂ + y₁)/(k + 1) ]
Points of Trisection: Dividing a line segment into three equal parts using ratios 1 : 2 and 2 : 1
subtopics: Proof of section formula via AAA similarity of projection triangles
Division by coordinate axes: Point on x-axis has y = 0, point on y-axis has x = 0
Parallelogram diagonal bisection theorem applied to coordinate geometry

worked_examples.problem: Example 6 (NCERT): Find the coordinates of the point which divides the line segment joining the points (4, -3) and (8, 5) in the ratio 3 : 1 internally.
worked_examples.solution:
Let A = (4, -3) and B = (8, 5).
Here x₁ = 4, y₁ = -3, x₂ = 8, y₂ = 5.
Given ratio m₁ : m₂ = 3 : 1.

Formula: Section Formula for internal division:
x = (m₁x₂ + m₂x₁) / (m₁ + m₂)
y = (m₁y₂ + m₂y₁) / (m₁ + m₂)

Step 1: Compute x-coordinate:
x = [ 3(8) + 1(4) ] / (3 + 1) = [ 24 + 4 ] / 4 = 28 / 4 = 7.

Step 2: Compute y-coordinate:
y = [ 3(5) + 1(-3) ] / (3 + 1) = [ 15 - 3 ] / 4 = 12 / 4 = 3.
[ROUGH_WORK]
x: (3×8 + 1×4)/4 = 28/4 = 7
y: (3×5 + 1×(-3))/4 = 12/4 = 3
Boxed Answer: [ The coordinates of the dividing point are P(7, 3) ].
concept_questions: Why does the ratio multiplier m₁ multiply the coordinate of B (x₂) and not A (x₁)?
What coordinates would you get if the ratio was 1 : 3 instead of 3 : 1?

worked_examples.problem: Example 7 (NCERT): In what ratio does the point (-4, 6) divide the line segment joining the points A(-6, 10) and B(3, -8)?
worked_examples.solution:
Let the required ratio be k : 1.
Here A(-6, 10) is (x₁, y₁), B(3, -8) is (x₂, y₂).
The dividing point is P(-4, 6).

Formula for x-coordinate with ratio k : 1:
x = (k x₂ + 1 x₁) / (k + 1)

Substitute known values:
-4 = [ k(3) + 1(-6) ] / (k + 1)
-4(k + 1) = 3k - 6
-4k - 4 = 3k - 6
-4k - 3k = -6 + 4
-7k = -2
k = 2/7.
Therefore, the ratio k : 1 is (2/7) : 1 = 2 : 7.

Verification with y-coordinate:
y = [ k y₂ + y₁ ] / (k + 1) = [ (2/7)(-8) + 10 ] / (2/7 + 1)
= [ -16/7 + 70/7 ] / (9/7) = (54/7) / (9/7) = 54 / 9 = 6.
Since y = 6 matches the given y-coordinate, the result is fully verified!
[ROUGH_WORK]
Ratio k : 1 reduces 2 variables (m₁, m₂) to 1 variable k!
Boxed Answer: [ The point P(-4, 6) divides segment AB internally in the ratio 2 : 7 ].
concept_questions: Why is setting the ratio as k : 1 algebraically superior to using m₁ : m₂?
What would it mean if k turned out to be negative?

title: Exercise 7.1 Complete Solver: Distance Formula Calculations & Collinearity Tests (Q1 to Q10)
description: Complete step-by-step resolution of NCERT Exercise 7.1 Questions 1 through 10. Master distance between points with symbolic parameters (a, b), Town A to Town B geographical distance, testing collinearity of (1, 5), (2, 3), (-2, -11), Champa-Chameli classroom grid square proof, quadrilateral classification, and finding points equidistant on coordinate axes.
key_concepts: Ex 7.1 Q3: Testing collinearity of A(1, 5), B(2, 3), C(-2, -11) ⇒ AB = √5, BC = √212, AC = √265 (Not collinear)
Ex 7.1 Q4: Testing isosceles triangle (5, -2), (6, 4), (7, -2)
Ex 7.1 Q5: Champa and Chameli classroom grid: A(3, 4), B(6, 7), C(9, 4), D(6, 1) forms a square
Ex 7.1 Q7: Point on x-axis (x, 0) equidistant from (2, -5) and (-2, 9) ⇒ x = -7 ⇒ (-7, 0)
Ex 7.1 Q8: Value of y for distance 10 between P(2, -3) and Q(10, y) ⇒ y = 3 or y = -9
Ex 7.1 Q9: Equidistant Q(0, 1) from P(5, -3) and R(x, 6)
Ex 7.1 Q10: Relation between x and y equidistant from (3, 6) and (-3, 4) ⇒ 3x + y - 5 = 0
subtopics: Full resolution of Q1 to Q10
Proving a figure is a square (all 4 sides equal AND both diagonals equal)
Solving quadratic equations arising from distance constraints

worked_examples.problem: Exercise 7.1 Q1 (iii): Find the distance between the points (a, b) and (-a, -b).
worked_examples.solution:
Let P = (a, b) and Q = (-a, -b).
Here x₁ = a, y₁ = b, x₂ = -a, y₂ = -b.

Formula: d = √[ (x₂ - x₁)² + (y₂ - y₁)² ]
Substitution:
d = √[ (-a - a)² + (-b - b)² ]
= √[ (-2a)² + (-2b)² ]
= √[ 4a² + 4b² ]
Factor out 4 from under the radical:
= √[ 4(a² + b²) ]
= 2 √(a² + b²).
[ROUGH_WORK]
(-2a)² = 4a²
√4 = 2
Boxed Answer: [ Distance = 2√(a² + b²) units ].
concept_questions: Why is the distance from the origin to (a, b) equal to half of this distance?
Notice the points (a, b) and (-a, -b) are diagonally opposite reflections through the origin!

worked_examples.problem: Exercise 7.1 Q7: Find the point on the x-axis which is equidistant from (2, -5) and (-2, 9).
worked_examples.solution:
Any point on the x-axis has its y-coordinate equal to 0.
Let the required point on the x-axis be P(x, 0).
Let given points be A(2, -5) and B(-2, 9).

Condition: PA = PB ⇒ PA² = PB²

Formula:
PA² = (x - 2)² + (0 - (-5))² = (x - 2)² + 5² = (x² - 4x + 4) + 25 = x² - 4x + 29
PB² = (x - (-2))² + (0 - 9)² = (x + 2)² + (-9)² = (x² + 4x + 4) + 81 = x² + 4x + 85

Equating PA² and PB²:
x² - 4x + 29 = x² + 4x + 85
Cancel x² from both sides:
-4x + 29 = 4x + 85
-4x - 4x = 85 - 29
-8x = 56
x = 56 / (-8) = -7.

Therefore, the required point is (-7, 0).
[ROUGH_WORK]
Check PA: √[(-7 - 2)² + (0 - (-5))²] = √[(-9)² + 5²] = √[81 + 25] = √106
Check PB: √[(-7 - (-2))² + (0 - 9)²] = √[(-5)² + (-9)²] = √[25 + 81] = √106
PA = PB = √106 (Verified!)
Boxed Answer: [ The point on the x-axis is (-7, 0) ].

How would you set up the problem if the point was on the y-axis instead?

worked_examples.problem: Exercise 7.1 Q8: Find the values of y for which the distance between the points P(2, -3) and Q(10, y) is 10 units.
worked_examples.solution:
Given: P = (2, -3), Q = (10, y). Distance PQ = 10 units.
Squaring both sides: PQ² = 10² = 100.

Formula: PQ² = (10 - 2)² + (y - (-3))²
100 = 8² + (y + 3)²
100 = 64 + (y + 3)²
(y + 3)² = 100 - 64 = 36

Taking square root on both sides:
y + 3 = ±√36 = ±6

Case 1: y + 3 = 6 ⇒ y = 6 - 3 = 3.
Case 2: y + 3 = -6 ⇒ y = -6 - 3 = -9.
[ROUGH_WORK]
Check y = 3: (10 - 2)² + (3 - (-3))² = 8² + 6² = 64 + 36 = 100 ⇒ √100 = 10 (True!)
Check y = -9: 8² + (-9 + 3)² = 8² + (-6)² = 64 + 36 = 100 ⇒ √100 = 10 (True!)
Boxed Answer: [ y = 3 or y = -9 ].

worked_examples.problem: Exercise 7.1 Q10: Find a relation between x and y such that the point (x, y) is equidistant from the point (3, 6) and (-3, 4).
worked_examples.solution:
Let P(x, y) be equidistant from A(3, 6) and B(-3, 4).
Condition: PA = PB ⇒ PA² = PB²

PA² = (x - 3)² + (y - 6)² = x² - 6x + 9 + y² - 12y + 36 = x² + y² - 6x - 12y + 45
PB² = (x - (-3))² + (y - 4)² = (x + 3)² + (y - 4)² = x² + 6x + 9 + y² - 8y + 16 = x² + y² + 6x - 8y + 25

Equating PA² and PB²:
x² + y² - 6x - 12y + 45 = x² + y² + 6x - 8y + 25
Cancel x² + y²:
-6x - 12y + 45 = 6x - 8y + 25
Move terms to RHS:
6x + 6x - 8y + 12y + 25 - 45 = 0
12x + 4y - 20 = 0
Divide entire equation by 4:
3x + y - 5 = 0.
[ROUGH_WORK]
Midpoint of AB: ((3 - 3)/2, (6 + 4)/2) = (0, 5).
Substitute (0, 5) into 3x + y - 5: 3(0) + 5 - 5 = 0 (True!)
Boxed Answer: [ The relation between x and y is 3x + y - 5 = 0 ].
concept_questions: What is the slope of the line segment AB, and what is the slope of 3x + y - 5 = 0? Verify they are negative reciprocals.

title: Exercise 7.2 Complete Solver: Section Formula, Trisection & Sports Day Flag Coordinates (Q1 to Q10)
description: Complete resolution of NCERT Exercise 7.2 Questions 1 through 10. Master trisection of line segments, the famous Sports Day green and red flag problem, finding unknown ratios from axes division, parallelogram 4th vertex determination, and area of a rhombus via diagonals.
key_concepts: Ex 7.2 Q1: Point dividing (-1, 7) and (4, -3) in ratio 2 : 3 ⇒ (1, 3)
Ex 7.2 Q2: Points of trisection of (4, -1) and (-2, -3) ⇒ P(2, -5/3) and Q(0, -7/3)
Ex 7.2 Q3: Sports Day: Niharika at (2, 25), Preet at (8, 20) ⇒ Distance = √61 m; Rashmi midpoint at (5, 22.5)
Ex 7.2 Q4: Ratio in which (-1, 6) divides (-3, 10) and (6, -8) ⇒ 2 : 7
Ex 7.2 Q5: Ratio in which x-axis divides (1, -5) and (-4, 5) ⇒ 1 : 1 (midpoint) ⇒ (-3/2, 0)
Ex 7.2 Q6: Vertices of parallelogram (1, 2), (4, y), (x, 6), (3, 5) ⇒ Equating diagonal midpoints ⇒ x = 6, y = 3
Ex 7.2 Q7: Coordinates of point A where AB is diameter of circle with center (2, -3) and B(1, 4) ⇒ A(3, -10)
Ex 7.2 Q8: Point P on AB such that AP = (3/7)AB ⇒ Ratio AP : PB = 3 : 4
Ex 7.2 Q9: Dividing segment joining (-2, 2) and (2, 8) into four equal parts
Ex 7.2 Q10: Area of rhombus with vertices taken in order = (1/2) × d₁ × d₂
subtopics: Full resolution of Q1 to Q10
Parallelogram property: Diagonals bisect each other ⇒ Midpoint of AC = Midpoint of BD
Rhombus area calculation via coordinate diagonal lengths

worked_examples.problem: Exercise 7.2 Q2: Find the coordinates of the points of trisection of the line segment joining (4, -1) and (-2, -3).
worked_examples.solution:
Let A = (4, -1) and B = (-2, -3).
Points of trisection P and Q divide segment AB into 3 equal parts: AP = PQ = QB.

Step 1: Point P divides AB internally in the ratio 1 : 2:
Here m₁ = 1, m₂ = 2.
x_P = [ 1(-2) + 2(4) ] / (1 + 2) = [ -2 + 8 ] / 3 = 6 / 3 = 2.
y_P = [ 1(-3) + 2(-1) ] / (1 + 2) = [ -3 - 2 ] / 3 = -5/3.
So P = (2, -5/3).

Step 2: Point Q divides AB internally in the ratio 2 : 1 (or Q is the midpoint of PB):
Using midpoint of PB:
x_Q = (x_P + x_B) / 2 = [ 2 + (-2) ] / 2 = 0 / 2 = 0.
y_Q = (y_P + y_B) / 2 = [ -5/3 + (-3) ] / 2 = [ -5/3 - 9/3 ] / 2 = (-14/3) / 2 = -7/3.
So Q = (0, -7/3).
[ROUGH_WORK]
Check Q via 2:1 on AB:
x = (2(-2) + 1(4))/3 = (-4 + 4)/3 = 0
y = (2(-3) + 1(-1))/3 = (-6 - 1)/3 = -7/3
Both methods give identical coordinates!
Boxed Answer: [ Coordinates of points of trisection are P(2, -5/3) and Q(0, -7/3) ].
concept_questions: Why does using the midpoint of PB for finding Q save computational time?
How many trisection points does a line segment have?

worked_examples.problem: Exercise 7.2 Q6: If (1, 2), (4, y), (x, 6) and (3, 5) are the vertices of a parallelogram taken in order, find x and y.
worked_examples.solution:
Let vertices of parallelogram ABCD in order be:
A(1, 2), B(4, y), C(x, 6), D(3, 5).

Fundamental Theorem: The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
Therefore: Midpoint of diagonal AC = Midpoint of diagonal BD.

Step 1: Find midpoint of AC:
Midpoint of AC = [ (1 + x)/2, (2 + 6)/2 ] = [ (1 + x)/2, 8/2 ] = [ (1 + x)/2, 4 ].

Step 2: Find midpoint of BD:
Midpoint of BD = [ (4 + 3)/2, (y + 5)/2 ] = [ 7/2, (y + 5)/2 ].

Step 3: Equate the respective coordinates of the midpoints:
x-coordinate:
(1 + x) / 2 = 7 / 2 ⇒ 1 + x = 7 ⇒ x = 6.

y-coordinate:
(y + 5) / 2 = 4 ⇒ y + 5 = 8 ⇒ y = 3.
[ROUGH_WORK]
Midpoint of AC: ((1+6)/2, 4) = (3.5, 4)
Midpoint of BD: (7/2, (3+5)/2) = (3.5, 4) (Verified!)
Boxed Answer: [ x = 6, y = 3 ].
concept_questions: Why is using the midpoint property infinitely faster than setting opposite sides equal with the distance formula?
What happens if the vertices are not taken in cyclic order?

worked_examples.problem: Exercise 7.2 Q8: If A and B are (-2, -2) and (2, -4), respectively, find the coordinates of P such that AP = 3/7 AB and P lies on the line segment AB.
worked_examples.solution:
Given: A = (-2, -2), B = (2, -4).
Given relation: AP = (3/7) AB.

Step 1: Determine the ratio AP : PB:
PB = AB - AP = AB - (3/7) AB = (4/7) AB.
Therefore:
AP / PB = [ (3/7) AB ] / [ (4/7) AB ] = 3 / 4.
So P divides segment AB internally in the ratio 3 : 4 (m₁ = 3, m₂ = 4).

Step 2: Apply Section Formula:
x = [ 3(2) + 4(-2) ] / (3 + 4) = [ 6 - 8 ] / 7 = -2/7.
y = [ 3(-4) + 4(-2) ] / (3 + 4) = [ -12 - 8 ] / 7 = -20/7.
[ROUGH_WORK]
Common pitfall: Taking ratio as 3 : 7 instead of 3 : 4!
AP is 3 parts out of 7 total parts, so PB is 4 parts!
Boxed Answer: [ Coordinates of P are (-2/7, -20/7) ].
concept_questions: Why is the ratio AP : PB equal to 3 : 4 and NOT 3 : 7?
What fraction of AB is PB?

        </g>
        
  
    <g transform="translate(50, 70)">
      <rect width="480" height="230" fill="#F8FAFC" stroke="#CBD5E1" stroke-width="1.5" rx="10"/>
      <text x="24" y="28" fill="#0F172A" font-size="14" font-weight="700">Class 10 Coordinate Geometry Governing Formulas</text>
      
      <!-- Distance Formula -->
      <rect x="24" y="44" width="432" height="48" fill="#EFF6FF" stroke="#93C5FD" rx="6"/>
      <text x="36" y="66" fill="#1E40AF" font-size="11" font-weight="700">1. Distance Formula:</text>
      <text x="36" y="84" fill="#2563EB" font-size="13" font-weight="700">d = √[ (x₂ - x₁)² + (y₂ - y₁)² ]   [From origin: d = √(x² + y²)]</text>

      <rect x="24" y="100" width="432" height="52" fill="#F0FDF4" stroke="#86EFAC" rx="6"/>
      <text x="36" y="120" fill="#166534" font-size="11" font-weight="700">2. Section Formula (Internal Division in m₁ : m₂):</text>
      <text x="36" y="140" fill="#15803D" font-size="13" font-weight="700">P(x, y) = [ (m₁x₂ + m₂x₁) / (m₁ + m₂),  (m₁y₂ + m₂y₁) / (m₁ + m₂) ]</text>

      <text x="36" y="198" fill="#B45309" font-size="12" font-weight="700">Midpoint M = [ (x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2 ] | Centroid G = [ Σx/3, Σy/3 ]</text>
    </g>
    
</svg>

title: Board Exam Analytic Mastery: Triangle Centroid, Collinear Parameterization & Rhombus Area
description: Master advanced board exam coordinate geometry problems. Rigorous derivation of the Centroid Formula G = [ (x₁+x₂+x₃)/3, (y₁+y₂+y₃)/3 ], finding circumcentre of a triangle from equidistant vertices, and calculating polygon areas via analytical decomposition.
key_concepts: Centroid of a Triangle Formula: G = [ (x₁ + x₂ + x₃)/3, (y₁ + y₂ + y₃)/3 ]
Centroid Division Ratio: The centroid G divides each median internally in the ratio 2 : 1 from vertex to base midpoint
Circumcentre Properties: Equidistant from all 3 vertices OA = OB = OC
Area of Rhombus Formula: Area = (1/2) × d₁ × d₂ using distance formula for diagonals AC and BD
Analytical Locus & Equidistant Constraints
subtopics: Derivation of the centroid formula using section formula on median
Finding circumcentre coordinates by solving linear system OA² = OB² = OC²
Full resolution of Exercise 7.2 Question 10 (Area of Rhombus)

worked_examples.problem: Derive the coordinates of the centroid G of a triangle whose vertices are A(x₁, y₁), B(x₂, y₂), and C(x₃, y₃).
worked_examples.solution:
STATEMENT: The centroid G of a triangle divides each median internally in the ratio 2 : 1.

Step 1: Find the coordinates of the midpoint D of base BC:
D is the midpoint of B(x₂, y₂) and C(x₃, y₃).
By Midpoint Formula:
D = [ (x₂ + x₃)/2, (y₂ + y₃)/2 ].

Step 2: Apply the Section Formula to median AD:
The centroid G divides median AD internally in the ratio 2 : 1 from vertex A to D.
Here m₁ = 2, m₂ = 1.
Point A is (x₁, y₁), and Point D is [ (x₂ + x₃)/2, (y₂ + y₃)/2 ].

Step 3: Calculate x-coordinate of G:
x_G = [ m₁ x_D + m₂ x_A ] / (m₁ + m₂)
= [ 2 × ((x₂ + x₃)/2) + 1 × x₁ ] / (2 + 1)
= [ (x₂ + x₃) + x₁ ] / 3
= (x₁ + x₂ + x₃) / 3.

Step 4: Calculate y-coordinate of G:
y_G = [ m₁ y_D + m₂ y_A ] / (m₁ + m₂)
= [ 2 × ((y₂ + y₃)/2) + 1 × y₁ ] / (2 + 1)
= [ (y₂ + y₃) + y₁ ] / 3
= (y₁ + y₂ + y₃) / 3.

Conclusion:
Centroid G = [ (x₁ + x₂ + x₃) / 3, (y₁ + y₂ + y₃) / 3 ].
Hence Derived!
[ROUGH_WORK]
2 cancels the /2 in the midpoint formula perfectly!
Boxed Answer: [ Centroid G = ( (x₁ + x₂ + x₃)/3, (y₁ + y₂ + y₃)/3 ) ].

What is the physical meaning of the centroid in physics (centre of gravity)?

worked_examples.problem: Exercise 7.2 Q10: Find the area of a rhombus if its vertices are (3, 0), (4, 5), (-1, 4) and (-2, -1) taken in order.
worked_examples.solution:
Let vertices in order be A(3, 0), B(4, 5), C(-1, 4), and D(-2, -1).
Formula: Area of a rhombus = (1/2) × d₁ × d₂ = (1/2) × AC × BD.

Step 1: Find length of diagonal AC:
AC = √[ (-1 - 3)² + (4 - 0)² ]
= √[ (-4)² + 4² ] = √[ 16 + 16 ] = √32 = 4√2 units.

Step 2: Find length of diagonal BD:
BD = √[ (-2 - 4)² + (-1 - 5)² ]
= √[ (-6)² + (-6)² ] = √[ 36 + 36 ] = √72 = 6√2 units.

Step 3: Calculate Area:
Area = (1/2) × AC × BD
= (1/2) × (4√2) × (6√2)
= (1/2) × 24 × (√2 × √2)
= (1/2) × 24 × 2 = 24 square units.
[ROUGH_WORK]
(4√2 × 6√2) / 2 = 24 × 2 / 2 = 24
Boxed Answer: [ Area of the rhombus = 24 square units ].
concept_questions: Why is the area of a rhombus equal to half the product of its diagonals?
Do the diagonals of a rhombus intersect at 90°? Check the slopes of AC and BD.
